title: Registered Disability Savings Plan
subtitle: Build long-term support without asking one deposit to perform a miracle

blocks.text: Long-term saving is rarely dramatic. Most days it is one sensible deposit wearing ordinary shoes, which is fortunate, because money in a cape usually comes with suspicious fees.

A Registered Disability Savings Plan helps a person approved for the Disability Tax Credit save for the long term. Money you put in can grow without tax until it comes out, and plans that qualify may get the Canada Disability Savings Grant and the Canada Disability Savings Bond. The beneficiary owns the future benefit, and the holder runs the plan under the rules.
The most anyone can put in over a lifetime is $200,000 for one beneficiary, across all of their RDSPs. Grants, bonds and investment growth do not count toward that limit.

items.title: “An RDSP is available to anyone who identifies as having a disability.”
items.text: The beneficiary normally must be approved for the Disability Tax Credit and meet the plan’s age, residence and ID rules. The RDSP does not run its own informal audition.

blocks.text: Learn who does what in an RDSP and how government money gets added, and you can build support that lasts for decades.
blocks.detail: Knowing the difference between the grant, the bond and your own contributions helps you put each dollar where it earns the most.
blocks.extra: Next, four clear roles so everyone knows their job.

sections.title: Give Every Role a Clear Name

items.title: BENEFICIARY
items.text: The person approved for the DTC whose savings are being built. Payments from the plan go to this person.

items.title: HOLDER
items.text: The person or group that opens and runs the plan. Depending on age and whether they can sign contracts, this may be the adult beneficiary or someone else who qualifies.

items.title: CONTRIBUTOR
items.text: The holder, or another person or group who adds money with the holder’s written OK. You cannot deduct contributions from your taxes, and the money is held for the beneficiary.

items.title: ISSUER
items.text: The bank or financial company that offers the RDSP. Products, investments and fees can differ, but the federal plan rules are the same.

blocks.text: You can keep adding money until the end of the year the beneficiary turns 59, as long as they still qualify and the $200,000 lifetime limit has not been reached.
There is no yearly limit on what you can put in. A large deposit made without checking your grant plan can use up lifetime room without getting the best match.

items.title: “Every dollar contributed receives the same government match.”
items.text: The grant can be 300%, 200% or 100%, depending on family income, how much you put in and what is left to claim. Once the best level is full, extra dollars may get a smaller grant or none.

sections.title: Separate the Grant From the Bond

blocks.text: The Canada Disability Savings Grant matches money you put in. The usual most you can get is $3,500 in one year and $70,000 over the beneficiary’s lifetime. The Canada Disability Savings Bond helps beneficiaries with low and modest incomes. You do not have to put in any money, and it pays up to $1,000 a year and $20,000 over a lifetime.
Grant and bond payments stop after December 31 of the year the beneficiary turns 49. Opening and checking the plan early leaves more years open for government help.

Grant and bond amounts you did not use in up to the past ten eligible years may be carried forward. The oldest amounts are used first, and there are yearly caps. Ask the issuer for the official Statement of Entitlement before you decide how much to put in.
The bond can be paid into a plan even if you add no money. A family waiting to save the perfect amount should still look into opening a plan.

items.title: “If ten years of unused entitlement exist, the government pays all of it immediately.”
items.text: Carry-forward is limited by eligibility, age, past income records and yearly grant or bond caps. It is a queue, not a wheelbarrow arriving at the branch.

blocks.text: Key takeaway
An RDSP is a long-term plan. Keep your DTC records safe, use grant and bond years before age 49, put money in with a plan, and learn the repayment rules for withdrawals.

Payments from an RDSP usually mix your own contributions, grants, bonds and growth. Your own contributions are not taxed when they come out. Grants, bonds and growth usually are. The issuer works out each part and reports it.

Taking money out can mean paying back grants and bonds from the past ten years. Under the proportional rule, you may have to repay $3 of government money for each $1 you take out, up to the amount being held back. Ask the issuer for a written estimate before you approve a withdrawal.

Lifetime Disability Assistance Payments must start by the end of the year the beneficiary turns 60. One-time Disability Assistance Payments may also be possible, under the plan’s terms and federal limits.

items.title: How do the beneficiary, holder and contributor roles differ?
items.detail: The beneficiary gets the plan’s future benefit, the holder opens and runs it, and a contributor with permission adds money.

items.title: Which government amount needs you to put money in, and which may not?
items.detail: The Canada Disability Savings Grant matches money you put in. The Canada Disability Savings Bond may be paid even if you add nothing.

items.title: What happens at the end of the year the beneficiary turns 49?
items.detail: Grant and bond payments stop after December 31 of that year.

items.title: What is the lifetime limit on money you can put in?
items.detail: $200,000 for one beneficiary across all of their RDSPs.

items.title: Why ask for a Statement of Entitlement before you put money in?
items.detail: It shows the grant and bond amounts you can get now and from past years, so you can time your deposits well.

sections.title: Noah and the Contribution That Tried to Sprint

blocks.text: Meet Noah
paragraphs: Noah Chen was 31 and had just opened his first RDSP. His goal was a plan that could support him for decades. His Aunt Mei wanted to help, and she did not wait. She sold her old car, and that same afternoon she showed up with a $20,000 cheque in her purse and one wish: put it all in this Friday.

Her heart was in exactly the right place. Her calculator had skipped warm-up. Noah knew just enough to worry. One big deposit would use up lifetime contribution room, and the grant only matches part of what goes in.
The adviser at the issuer said the cheque could go in as soon as Friday. Aunt Mei was already smiling. "Why wait?" she said. "Money in the plan is money working."

Noah felt the pull. Saying no to his aunt, who had just sold her car for him, felt rude. But he remembered one rule from his notes: ask for the Statement of Entitlement first. He took a breath and asked her to hold the cheque for one week. She went quiet for a moment, then nodded.

The statement showed two things they had not expected. Noah had unused grant amounts from earlier eligible years that could be carried forward, but only up to yearly caps. And he qualified for the bond, which needed no contribution at all. A $20,000 deposit would have filled the best matching tiers and then kept going, using up lifetime room on dollars that earned little or no match.

They planned a smaller first deposit, sized to the match available that year, with more to follow while carry-forward lasted. The bond arrived with no contribution. Aunt Mei kept the rest of her car money in her own account and put the later dates on her calendar.

Noah wrote down one more thing: a withdrawal in the next ten years could mean repaying grants and bonds. Then he put the statement in a folder. Aunt Mei took the cheque home and, to her credit, only sighed twice.

blocks.text: A family gift should start with permission, clear roles and the beneficiary’s long-term needs. More money today is not always better than a plan that runs over several years.
Noah's aunt wanted to deposit $20,000 on Friday. One week and one statement changed the plan.
blocks.detail: Asking for the Statement of Entitlement first showed him where a deposit would earn a match and where it would not.
blocks.extra: Last stop: your own long-term support blueprint.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Long-Term Support Blueprint

blocks.text: Short answers in plain words. Please do not enter your SIN, banking details or plan account numbers. This is preparation, not investment or tax advice.

Before you choose an investment, compare fees, access, risk and how long the money will stay in. “Registered” describes the account’s tax rules. It does not make every investment inside it a good one.

items.title: Beneficiary
items.text: The person the plan is set up for and paid to.

items.title: Holder
items.text: The person or organization that manages the plan.

items.title: CDSG
items.text: Canada Disability Savings Grant. It matches money you put in.

items.title: CDSB
items.text: Canada Disability Savings Bond. You may not need to put in any money to get it.

items.title: Carry-forward
items.text: Using grant or bond amounts you did not use in earlier years.

items.title: Assistance holdback
items.text: Recent grants and bonds you may have to pay back after a withdrawal.

quiz.question: True or False: “An RDSP is available to anyone who identifies as having a disability.”

questions: Is the person the plan is for approved for the Disability Tax Credit? (Yes / No / Not sure)
How old is the beneficiary? A rough age is fine.
Does an RDSP already exist for this person? (Yes / No / Not sure)
Who would open the plan, and who might add money to it?
About how much could you or your family add each year? An estimate is fine. “Nothing right now” is a fine answer too.
What is one thing you will do before you add money or take any out?
samples: Yes, I opened one this year.
I opened it. My aunt wants to add money.
Ask the issuer for my Statement of Entitlement.
